questions.question: Describe the input and the required output of a PET recycling plant and explain why the economics are tight.
questions.expected_answer: The input is bales of crushed PET bottles bought from buy-back centres, dirty, mixed in colour, with caps, labels, some wrong plastics and occasional stones or bricks added for weight. The required output is clean, dry, uniform pellets, sorted by colour, free of PVC and other specks, that a bottle or fibre maker will buy; a pellet that fails the buyer's standard is worth almost nothing. The economics are tight because the price of recycled pellet follows the price of new plastic, which follows the oil price, while the plant must pay for collecting, sorting labour, water, electricity, chemicals and machines; producer responsibility fees and bottle makers' commitments to use recycled content keep the plants viable.

questions.question: List, in order, the steps by which a bale of bottles becomes pellets, stating what each step removes or changes.
questions.expected_answer: One, the bale is opened and sorted by hand or sensor to remove non-PET items and to separate clear from coloured bottles. Two, a drum strips labels and loose dirt. Three, a granulator shreds the bottles into flake about a centimetre across. Four, a hot wash with caustic soda and detergent removes glue, sugar, soil and oil, and a float-sink tank separates sinking PET from floating cap and label plastics. Five, the flake is rinsed and hot-air dried, because moisture would break the chains in the melt, and is tested for colour, PVC specks and moisture. Six, an extruder melts the flake at about 270 degrees, pushes it through a fine screen to catch specks and through a die, and the cooled strands are chopped into pellets, which are tested and bagged; food-grade pellet gets a further high-temperature vacuum decontamination.

questions.question: Draw and label a systems diagram for a plastics recycling project and explain the purpose of the feedback loop.
questions.expected_answer: The diagram has three boxes from left to right joined by arrows: input, bales of waste bottles; process, the chain sort, wash, shred, float-sink, dry, extrude, pelletise, listed in order inside the box; and output, clean pellets. Resources, water, electricity, caustic soda, labour and machines, are shown entering the process from above, and waste streams, floated caps and labels, dirt, waste water and rejects, leaving below. A feedback arrow runs from the quality tests at the output back to the process. The feedback loop carries the test results, for colour, moisture or contamination, back to the stage responsible, such as sorting or drying, so that the process can be corrected; without it the plant could not detect or fix a failing batch, and the same loop, testing against specifications, applies to any design project.
